HELD-OUT PROSE FOR PERPLEXITY MEASUREMENT

Written for this repository on 2026-08-10 rather than taken from wikitext or
Project Gutenberg. Those corpora sit in the training set of every model this
engine runs, which deflates perplexity by an unknown amount and turns the
absolute number into a fiction. Original text is not a guarantee of novelty —
nothing written in English is truly out of distribution — but it removes the
worst of the contamination, and the number is only ever used comparatively.

Length is a measurement property, not an editorial one. The file is sized past
four thousand tokens because the block standard error of a perplexity run falls
with the number of roughly independent 64-token blocks in it, and a corpus that
runs out caps the precision of every run no matter how large --tokens gets. The
registers below vary on purpose — essay, narrative, specification, transcript,
checklist — because a single voice measures a model's fit to that voice.

---

The harbour at Kaleköy silts up a little more each winter. Fishermen who have
worked the channel for thirty years describe the change as a narrowing rather
than a shallowing: the water still reaches the same depth at the mouth, but
the usable lane between the sandbar and the eastern rocks has drawn in from
roughly forty metres to something closer to twenty-five. Nobody has surveyed
it. The estimate circulates among the boats as a shared piece of practical
knowledge, revised each season, and it is accurate enough that a captain who
ignores it will ground his keel within a year.

There is a particular kind of engineering problem that resembles this. The
constraint is real, everyone working near it has a serviceable estimate, and
the estimate is never written down because writing it down would require
committing to a precision nobody has. So it propagates by apprenticeship. A
new engineer learns that a certain buffer should be about a gigabyte, or that
a certain retry count should be three, and the reason erodes until only the
number survives. Years later somebody asks where the number came from and
discovers that the last person who knew has left.

The failure mode is not that the number is wrong. Often it is approximately
right, for the same reason the fishermen's estimate is approximately right:
it was calibrated against reality by people who paid for being wrong. The
failure mode is that the number stops tracking the reality it was calibrated
against. The channel keeps silting. The hardware gets larger. The workload
changes shape. And a constant that was a reasonable summary of the world in
one year becomes, silently and without any error message, a bad summary of
the world in the next.

What makes this hard to catch is that nothing breaks. A buffer that is too
small for its workload does not crash; it simply fails to hold what it could
have held, and the cost appears somewhere else entirely, as latency or as a
capability the team assumed was impossible. There is no test that fires. The
system reports success. Somebody looking at the code sees a plausible number
next to a plausible comment and moves on, and the comment is often the problem
— an explanation of what the number does is not an explanation of why it is
that number, and the two are almost impossible to tell apart when reading
quickly.

Ellen Toussaint, who spent eleven years maintaining a scheduling system for a
regional rail operator, used to keep a file she called the ledger. It listed
every magic number in the codebase, who chose it, what measurement or argument
produced it, and — this was the part she considered essential — what would
have to change in the world for the number to become wrong. Most entries were
short. Some said only "guessed, never measured, replace when it matters."
She maintained that the honest entries were the valuable ones, because they
told you where to look first when something started behaving strangely.

The rail operator's system carried a delay threshold of four minutes, below
which a train was considered on time and above which it triggered a cascade
of rebooking logic. The number came from a regulatory definition written in
the 1980s. By the time Toussaint inherited the system, the regulation had
changed twice, the rolling stock had been replaced, and the average journey
had shortened by about a fifth — but the threshold had not moved, because it
was not obviously broken, and because moving it would have required somebody
to argue for a specific alternative in a meeting. Her ledger entry for it read:
"1980s regulation, superseded 1997 and 2011. Almost certainly too generous.
Nobody wants to own the new value."

She was, she said later, never able to get it changed. What the ledger
achieved instead was smaller and more durable: when the rebooking logic began
misfiring during a timetable revision, the team found the entry in an
afternoon rather than reverse-engineering the threshold's provenance over a
fortnight. The number stayed wrong. The cost of its wrongness became visible.

There is an argument, which Toussaint made often and which is worth taking
seriously, that most of what passes for technical debt is really this: not bad
code, but unattributed decisions. Bad code announces itself. It is ugly, it is
slow, it fails under load, and somebody eventually rewrites it. An
unattributed decision looks exactly like a good decision. It sits in the
codebase wearing the same clothes. The only way to distinguish them is to ask
where the number came from, and by the time anybody thinks to ask, the answer
is usually gone.

The fishermen at Kaleköy have an advantage here that software teams do not.
Their estimate is re-derived every season, by everyone, under conditions where
being wrong is immediate and expensive. Nobody inherits the number; they
inherit the practice of measuring it. That is a more robust arrangement than
any ledger, and it is available to engineering teams far less often than one
would like, because most of the constants in a system are never tested against
anything that would push back.

---

NARRATIVE

The proofing cabinet at Halvorsen's went cold on a Tuesday in February, which
was the worst possible morning for it, because Tuesday was the day the hotel
took its standing order of ninety rolls and the hotel had never once tolerated
a late delivery. Ida found the cabinet at four in the morning, opened the door
out of habit rather than suspicion, and felt the wrong kind of air come out —
still, room-temperature, faintly sour. Six trays of dough sat there in a state
she could only describe afterwards as sulking. They had risen perhaps a third
of the way and then stopped, and the surfaces had gone slack and shiny, the way
dough does when it has been left to think about things for too long.

Her first instinct was to call Marek, who owned the bakery and who would be
asleep, and her second instinct — the one she followed — was to look at the
thermometer. It read nineteen degrees. The dial on the front of the cabinet
read twenty-eight, which was where it always read, because the dial was a
setting and not a measurement, a distinction Ida had understood in principle
for two years and understood properly for the first time at four in the
morning with ninety rolls to make.

She moved the trays to the top of the oven, which was still warm from the
previous night's bake and which was, she guessed, somewhere around twenty-four
degrees at the surface. Then she made a second batch from scratch, because she
did not trust the first one to recover, and because making a second batch was
something she could do with her hands while the rest of the problem sat there
being insoluble. Flour, water, salt, the tin of yeast from the cold room. She
worked fast and without much thought and got the second batch mixed by five.

The cabinet, it turned out, had not failed. Its heating element was fine. What
had failed was a small plastic clip inside the door, which had cracked at some
point in the previous week and which held the door magnet a few millimetres
proud of its seat, so that the door looked shut, felt shut, latched with the
familiar sound of a door shutting, and stood open by a gap you could not see
unless you crouched and put your eye level with the frame. The element had run
all night. The heat had gone out of the gap all night. The thermostat, which
measured the air inside and had no opinion about doors, had reported a room
that was doing its best.

Marek arrived at six and found two batches of dough, one recovering on the
oven top and one rising properly in the cold room, and Ida sitting on an
upturned crate with the broken clip in her palm. He looked at the clip for a
while. Then he said the thing she remembered for years afterwards, which was
that the cabinet had been telling the truth the entire time, and the trouble
was that nobody had asked it a question it was capable of answering.

They made the hotel delivery at half past seven, twenty minutes late, using the
recovered dough for sixty of the rolls and the fresh batch for the rest. Nobody
at the hotel noticed, or if they noticed they did not say. Ida replaced the
clip that afternoon with one she cut out of an old chopping board, and she also
did something that Marek thought was excessive at the time and endorsed later:
she taped a cheap glass thermometer to the inside of the cabinet door, at eye
level, where anyone opening it in the dark would see the number before they saw
the dough. It cost almost nothing. It answered a different question than the
thermostat did, and it answered it to a person instead of to a control loop.

Nine years later the bakery had four cabinets and a proper monitoring system
with alarms that went to Marek's phone, and every one of the four still had a
glass thermometer taped to the inside of the door.

---

TECHNICAL DESCRIPTION

The Vessen tide-gauge network, as it was rebuilt between the second and third
surveys, consists of forty-one stations distributed along roughly three hundred
kilometres of coastline, each reporting a water-level sample once every sixty
seconds. A station is a stilling well — a vertical pipe about two metres long,
open to the sea through a constriction at the base — with a float inside it and
a shaft encoder on the float's line. The constriction is the whole trick: it
admits the slow rise and fall of the tide almost unimpeded while damping the
faster oscillation of surface waves, so the float reports mean water level
rather than the height of whatever swell happens to be passing.

The choice of constriction diameter sets the time constant of that damping. A
narrow orifice damps aggressively and gives a very clean signal, at the cost of
lagging the true level during rapid changes — which matters during storm surge,
which is precisely when the network is most worth having. Vessen's stations use
a nominal twelve-millimetre orifice against a well diameter of one hundred and
sixty millimetres, giving a settling time on the order of forty seconds for a
step of one metre. Six stations in the northern group use eight millimetres
instead. Those six sit in exposed positions where the wave field is severe
enough that the cleaner damping was judged worth the additional lag, and the
processing chain corrects for the difference by station identifier rather than
by measurement, which is a compromise the survey documentation is explicit
about and mildly unhappy with.

Each encoder produces a 14-bit absolute position, which over the well's
two-metre travel yields a resolution of about 0.12 millimetres. This is far
finer than the accuracy of the instrument, which is limited by well dynamics,
thermal expansion of the float line, and the slow biological fouling of the
orifice, and which the survey characterises as plus or minus eight millimetres
under ordinary conditions. Reporting a value to a tenth of a millimetre when
the true uncertainty is eight is not dishonest so long as the uncertainty
travels with the value, and the record format requires it to: every sample
carries a quality byte, and the ingest rejects any sample whose quality byte is
absent rather than assuming a default.

Samples travel over a two-wire loop shared by all stations in a group, at 1200
baud, using a polling scheme in which the collector addresses each station in
turn and waits up to 250 milliseconds for a reply. A group of seven stations
therefore completes a full poll in under two seconds in the ordinary case and
in under four seconds in the worst case where every station has gone silent.
The 1200-baud figure is inherited from the original 1974 installation and is
absurd by any modern standard; it survives because the loop is nine kilometres
of buried copper of unknown provenance, because two attempts to characterise
its bandwidth produced contradictory results, and because nothing in the
requirement asks for more than one sample per station per minute. The survey's
own note on this reads: "Slow, proven, and not the bottleneck. Replace the
copper before replacing the modulation."

Fouling is the dominant maintenance cost. A stilling well in temperate water
accumulates growth at the orifice at a rate that varies enormously by season
and site, and a partially occluded orifice does not fail — it lengthens the
time constant. The station keeps reporting. The values remain plausible. What
changes is the phase of the reported tide relative to the true tide, by an
amount that grows from negligible to several minutes over a period of months.
This is detected, when it is detected, by comparing each station's phase
against the harmonic prediction for its location and flagging drift beyond four
minutes. The threshold is not derived from anything; it was chosen in 2011 by a
technician who observed that real fouling events crossed it and ordinary noise
did not, and it has been left alone since because it continues to behave that
way. It is a good example of a number that is defensible without being
principled.

---

TRANSCRIPT

The following is an excerpt from an internal review conducted after the loss of
a survey buoy. Speaker A is the review lead; speaker B is the deck officer who
performed the deployment; speaker C is the equipment technician.

A: I want to be clear at the start that this is not about assigning fault. The
buoy is gone, it cost what it cost, and the useful thing now is understanding
the sequence. Can you walk me through the deployment from the point where you
came onto the aft deck?

B: Sure. We were about forty minutes behind schedule because the winch had
tripped its overload on the previous cast, so there was some pressure to get on
with it. I came aft at about half two. The buoy was already on the rail with
the strop rigged. I checked the strop, checked the shackle, checked the release
was cocked, and gave the signal.

A: You checked the release was cocked. How?

B: Visually. There's a window on the housing, and when it's cocked you can see
a green band through it.

C: Can I come in there? The green band tells you the actuator has returned to
its home position. It doesn't tell you the pin has engaged. Those are two
different things and they're usually the same thing.

A: Usually.

C: Usually. The pin engages off a spring. If the spring is weak, or if there's
salt in the channel, the actuator can home and the pin can sit proud. You get
green in the window either way.

A: Was that documented anywhere?

C: It's in the manufacturer's service bulletin from — I want to say four years
ago. It's not in our deployment checklist.

A: Why not?

C: Honestly? Because the checklist was written before the bulletin, and nobody
owns the checklist. It gets copied from the last cruise's version. I've added
things to it twice by just editing the copy and hoping it propagates.

A: Did it propagate?

C: Once, yes. Once, no.

B: I'd like to say something about the forty minutes, if that's all right. I
don't think it changed what I checked. I think it changed how long I looked at
what I checked. There's a difference between running through a list and
actually seeing each item, and when you're behind, the list still gets run
through.

A: That's a useful distinction. Do you have a sense of how much time the full
check takes when you are actually seeing each item?

B: Ninety seconds, maybe two minutes. It's not long. That's what's frustrating.
It's not that I skipped a two-minute check to save two minutes, it's that
under pressure the check compresses on its own and you don't notice it
compressing.

A: Right. And the release fired when?

B: About eleven seconds after the buoy went over. Well before the depth trigger.

C: Which is consistent with the pin sitting proud and the load doing the rest.
It wouldn't have taken much.

A: Is there a way to check the pin rather than the actuator?

C: There is. You put a load on the release before deployment — a hand pull on
the strop, ten or fifteen kilos, which the pin holds easily if it's engaged and
which drops the strop immediately if it isn't. It takes about four seconds and
it tests the thing you actually care about instead of the thing that's easy to
see.

A: Then that goes in the checklist. And somebody owns the checklist.

C: I'll own it.

A: Write down that you own it, or in six months it will be nobody again.

---

CHECKLIST AND PROCEDURE

The revised pre-deployment sequence, in the order it is to be performed. Each
step is either an observation or an action; steps that are observations record a
value, and a step with no recorded value counts as not performed.

  1. Confirm the sea state against the deployment limit. Record the observed
     significant wave height and the limit in force. Do not proceed on a
     judgement that conditions are "about the same as yesterday."
  2. Inspect the strop along its full length. Look for glazing, for broken
     yarns at the eye, and for any stiffness that suggests a core failure.
  3. Shackle: correct size, pin fully seated, mousing wire present and intact.
  4. Release housing: green band visible through the window.
  5. Release load test. Apply a steady hand load of ten to fifteen kilograms to
     the strop for a slow count of four. The strop must not move. If it moves,
     the deployment stops here and the release is replaced, not adjusted.
  6. Confirm the depth trigger setting against the station plan. Record both.
  7. Confirm that the recovery beacon is transmitting, by receiving it, not by
     observing that its indicator light is on.
  8. Clear the deck of loose gear within two metres of the rail.
  9. Confirm that everyone on the aft deck is wearing a harness and that both
     tethers are clipped to hard points, not to the rail.
 10. Signal, deploy, and hold station until the first depth report arrives.

Items that must be aboard before the vessel sails, verified against this list by
two people independently:

  - Two complete release assemblies per planned deployment, plus one spare for
    the cruise as a whole.
  - Spring kits and channel grease for the release, sufficient for full service
    of every assembly aboard.
  - Strops: one per deployment plus two spares, each with its certificate.
  - Shackles and mousing wire, in the sizes the station plans call for and not
    merely in the sizes that were left over from the previous cruise.
  - The current deployment checklist, printed, laminated, and dated. A version
    on somebody's laptop does not satisfy this item.
  - The service bulletin file, complete to date.
  - A calibrated spring balance for step 5, so that "ten to fifteen kilograms"
    can be verified at least once per cruise rather than estimated by feel every
    time.

Three failure modes this sequence is specifically intended to catch, listed so
that a future reader can judge whether it still catches them:

  - A release that reports ready and is not, which is what was lost.
  - A strop that has been degraded by ultraviolet exposure on deck, which does
    not look degraded and loses a large fraction of its strength.
  - A depth trigger left at the previous station's setting, which produces a
    deployment that succeeds visibly and fails invisibly, returning data from
    the wrong depth.

---

CLOSING

What connects a bakery, a stilling well and a lost buoy is not that somebody was
careless. In each case a competent person looked at an indicator that was
working correctly and drew a conclusion the indicator did not support. The dial
reported a setting. The window reported an actuator. The thermostat reported the
temperature of air in a box whose door was open. None of these instruments lied.
They answered narrower questions than the questions being asked of them, and the
gap between the two questions was invisible precisely because the instrument was
in good order.

The remedy in each case was small and slightly redundant: a glass thermometer
taped where a person would see it, a four-second pull on a strop, a phase
comparison against a harmonic prediction. None of these replaced the existing
instrument. Each of them measured the same underlying thing by a different
route, so that the two could disagree. A single measurement, however precise,
cannot tell you that it is measuring the wrong quantity. Two measurements that
should agree can.

This is an expensive habit, and it is worth being honest that it does not scale
without limit. Every redundant check has a cost in time, in equipment, and in
the attention it takes from something else. The reason to build one is not that
redundancy is virtuous; it is that a specific failure has been identified whose
signature is agreement between an instrument and reality that has quietly
stopped being true. Where no such failure is plausible, the second measurement
is ceremony, and ceremony erodes the credibility of the checks that matter.

Which brings the argument back to the ledger. What Toussaint was really
recording, in the entries she considered honest, was the conditions under which
a number would stop being right. That is the same discipline as taping a
thermometer to a door: it is an admission that the thing you are relying on is
a proxy, plus a note about when the proxy might fail. Neither practice prevents
the failure. Both of them shorten, sometimes from a fortnight to an afternoon,
the interval between the failure happening and somebody being able to see it.
